steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (linguistic relativity): the language we speak shapes how we think. Strong version (linguistic determinism): language completely determines thought. Weak version (linguistic relativity): language influences thought but doesn't completely determine it.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Piaget's view: thought precedes language. Children must understand a concept before they can use the word for it (e.g. they must understand conservation before they can talk about it). Language reflects cognitive development rather than driving it.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Vygotsky's view: language enables thought. Inner speech (talking to yourself) develops from social speech and helps organise thinking. Language and thought initially develop separately, then merge around age 2 - language becomes a tool for thinking.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Evidence for language influencing thought: the Dani tribe had only two colour terms yet could discriminate between colours (Heider & Rosch) - challenges the strong version. However, English speakers find it easier to remember colours they have names for - supports the weak version.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis and evaluate the strong and weak versions. | Compare Piaget's and Vygotsky's views on the relationship between language and thought. | Evaluate whether language determines how we think, using research evidence.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Strong Sapir-Whorf = language DETERMINES thought (discredited). Weak = language INFLUENCES thought (supported). Piaget: thought -> language. Vygotsky: language -> thought. Remember: Piaget = Prepare (thought first), Vygotsky = Verbalise (language first). Always give SPECIFIC evidence when evaluating the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (e.g. colour studies, bilingualism).
